A first component of this size shows that one main effect runs through the whole data set rather than several independent effects.

The loadings show what that effect is. The positive end of the first component was defined by total antioxidant activity (1.005), total phenol (0.968), total flavonoid (0.942), total soluble sugar (0.905) and overall acceptability (0.874), and the negative end by total carbohydrate (-0.988), non-resistant starch (-0.965), starch (-0.963), lightness (-0.927), yellowness (-0.893), chroma (-0.888), springiness (-0.875) and amylose (-0.836). This is the same dilution gradient seen in the correlation matrix, since adding a vegetable extract removes starch and adds pigment in one step, so all these parameters must move together in a fixed pattern (Chhikara et al., 2019). The first component can therefore be described as a fortification axis. A single dominant component of this kind is common in fortified and fermented cereal products, where one processing step alters many characters at once (Granato et al., 2018).

The second component carried a much smaller share of the variation. Its positive end was defined by total protein (0.922), aroma (0.658), manganese (0.617), gumminess (0.608) and hardness (0.592), and its negative end by resistant starch (-0.783), beta-carotene (-0.644) and total colour difference (-0.590). This axis separates the carrot fortified treatments from the rest. The probable reason is that the two fortifying materials behave differently. Carrot supplies carotenoid and dietary fibre but very little free sugar, so it raises beta-carotene and resistant starch and leaves the product firmer, whereas beetroot supplies free sugar and betalain instead (Sharma et al., 2012). The second component therefore describes the difference between the two vegetables rather than any difference between the varieties.

The biplot presents the same result in picture form. Treatments lying close together have a similar quality profile, and a treatment lying near a vector is high in that parameter (Jolliffe, 2002). The twelve treatments separated into three clear groups along the first component in the order plain, carrot fortified and beet fortified, while the four varieties fell in the same order within every group, namely Dudeshwar, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira. This means that fortification decided the broad position of a treatment and variety decided its position within the group, so fortification was the stronger factor and variety the weaker one. KBI took the extreme positive position, close to the phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant and anthocyanin vectors, and DI the extreme negative position, close to the starch, carbohydrate and lightness vectors. The two years of each treatment always fell close together, most probably because the treatment effects were repeatable across the two seasons, and this provides independent support for pooling the data. A similar use of the method was made by Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026), who applied principal component analysis to twenty seven colour, textural and nutritional attributes of idli and used the position of the products on the biplot to identify the most promising formulations.

Cluster analysis was carried out on the standardised values of the forty two parameters of the twelve treatment combinations in order to group the treatments according to their overall quality. The squared Euclidean distance was used as the measure of dissimilarity and the groups were formed by the minimum variance method of Ward (1963), which is widely used for food quality data because it gives compact groups of nearly equal size (Everitt et al., 2011). The dendrogram is given in Fig. 4.46, the composition of the clusters in Table 4.46 and the cluster means in Table 4.47. The cophenetic correlation coefficient was 0.793, which shows that the dendrogram represents the original distance matrix reasonably well (Murtagh and Legendre, 2014).

The twelve treatments formed four clusters at a linkage distance of about 9.4. Cluster I contained the three plain products of the aromatic landraces, namely GI, KI and RI. Cluster II contained DI alone. Cluster III contained all four carrot fortified products and Cluster IV all four beet fortified products. The important point is that the first division was decided by fortification and not by variety, since all four beet fortified treatments grouped together whatever the parent variety, and the same was true of the carrot fortified treatments. This confirms the result of the principal component analysis, namely that the type of fortification is the main source of variation in product quality. Variety mattered only at the second level, where the plain product of the non-aromatic check separated from the plain products of the three aromatic landraces and formed a cluster of its own. This separation is itself informative, because it shows that the quality of the non-aromatic check departs from that of the aromatic landraces more than any two aromatic landraces depart from each other.

The cluster means describe the four groups clearly. Cluster IV, the beet fortified group, recorded the highest total phenol (265.22 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹), total flavonoid (142.75 mg QE 100 g⁻¹), total antioxidant activity (393.44 mg TE 100 g⁻¹), total soluble protein (2.24 per cent), calcium (500.89 mg L⁻¹), anthocyanin (1.41) and overall acceptability (8.06), with the lowest amylose, starch, total carbohydrate and lightness. Cluster III, the carrot fortified group, was intermediate for the bioactive fractions but recorded by far the highest beta-carotene (38.85), the highest resistant starch among the fortified groups (1.69 per cent), the lowest predicted glycaemic index (60.49) and the highest redness (11.57). Cluster I, the plain aromatic group, showed high starch, the highest total protein (13.09 per cent), the greatest hardness (114.11) and a moderate acceptability of 7.28. Cluster II, made up of DI alone, recorded the highest amylose, starch and total carbohydrate and the lowest total phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant activity and overall acceptability (6.14). On this basis Cluster IV is the group of choice where a functional product of high antioxidant value and high acceptability is wanted, and Cluster III where a provitamin A rich product of low glycaemic response is wanted.

The present experiment was undertaken to evaluate the sensory and nutritional quality of idli prepared from three traditional aromatic rice landraces of West Bengal, namely Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal and Kalojira, along with the non-aromatic check Dudeshwar, each used plain and fortified with carrot or beet extract. The experiment was laid out in a two factor completely randomised design with three replications and was repeated in two consecutive years, giving twelve treatment combinations and forty two quality parameters. The salient findings are summarised below.

Pooling of the data was justified by the Bartlett chi-square test, which was non-significant for all but four characters. For manganese, ash, PGI and springiness an Aitken transformation was applied before analysis. The experiment was precise, the coefficient of variation remaining below 3 per cent for most characters, with the lowest values for calcium (0.20 per cent) and total phenol and antioxidant activity (0.34 per cent each). The variety and product interaction was highly significant for the great majority of the nutritional, mineral, colour and textural characters, showing that the four varieties did not respond identically to fortification. It was non-significant only for taste, texture, appearance, cooking quality and overall acceptability.

Among the carbohydrate fractions, amylose ranged from 16.75 per cent in DI to 9.78 per cent in RBI, placing every combination in the low amylose class. Starch fell from 51.66 per cent in DI to 24.05 per cent in GBI and total carbohydrate from 60.21 to 40.91 per cent, while total soluble sugar rose in the opposite direction from 0.53 per cent in RI to 3.83 per cent in RBI. Resistant starch was highest in DCI (1.97 per cent) and the predicted glycaemic index lowest in RCI (58.46) and highest in KBI (75.08), the carrot fortified treatments consistently giving the most favourable glycaemic profile.

Among the proximate constituents, total soluble protein ranged from 2.71 per cent in KBI to 1.05 per cent in DI and total protein from 13.44 per cent in KI to 10.92 per cent in DCI, the three aromatic landraces exceeding the non-aromatic check throughout. Fat was uniformly low at 0.17 to 0.28 per cent, as expected of a steamed product. Ash ranged from 5.21 per cent in GBI to 2.47 per cent in DI and phytate from 2.52 mg g⁻¹ in KBI to 0.82 mg g⁻¹ in GI, both being highest in the beet fortified treatments.

The bioactive fractions showed the widest variation of any group of characters. Total phenol ranged from 290.97 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹ in KBI to 53.47 mg GAE 100 g⁻¹ in DI, a difference of more than five fold, and total flavonoid and total antioxidant activity followed the same order, from 171.34 to 42.95 mg QE 100 g⁻¹ and from 426.88 to 165.26 mg TE 100 g⁻¹ respectively. Beta-carotene was contributed almost entirely by carrot, reaching 45.77 in KCI against nil in every plain treatment, while anthocyanin was recorded only in the beet fortified treatments, reaching 1.86 in KBI.

Among the minerals, calcium showed the greatest response to fortification, rising from 61.44 mg L⁻¹ in KI to 550.88 mg L⁻¹ in GBI. Copper was highest in GBI (0.97 mg L⁻¹), iron and zinc in RI (3.36 and 0.89 mg L⁻¹) and manganese in GI (0.69 mg L⁻¹). Manganese was the only character for which the main effect of fortification was not significant.

Fortification altered the colour of the product markedly. Lightness fell from 72.92 in DI to 36.47 in DBI, redness rose from -1.81 in DI to 13.26 in DCI and yellowness fell from 110.98 to 59.45. The total colour difference ranged from 28.70 to 45.02, in every case far above the threshold at which a change becomes visible to an untrained eye. The texture was correspondingly softened, hardness falling from 147.73 in KI to 45.09 in DI, springiness from 1.04 to 0.46 and gumminess and chewiness from 11890.93 and 10263.60 in KI to their lowest values in KBI.

On the sensory panel, aroma was scored highest in GI (7.70) and lowest in KCI (5.65), showing that the vegetable extract partly masks the native aroma of the rice. For every other attribute the fortified treatments were superior, overall acceptability ranging from 8.64 in KBI to 6.14 in DI. The non-significant interaction for the main sensory attributes established that the benefit of fortification was of the same magnitude in all four varieties.

The multivariate analyses reinforced these findings. Correlation showed that overall acceptability was governed chiefly by colour and texture, being negatively related to total carbohydrate (r = -0.895) and positively to total flavonoid (r = 0.782). Principal component analysis extracted a first component explaining 50.12 per cent of the variation, which separated the plain, carrot fortified and beet fortified products along a single fortification gradient. Cluster analysis grouped the twelve treatments into four clusters in which the first division was again decided by fortification and not by variety, the plain product of the non-aromatic check standing apart as a cluster of its own.

It may be concluded from the present experiment that the variety, the type of fortification and their interaction all exert a significant influence on the nutritional, mineral, colour, textural and sensory quality of idli prepared from aromatic rice, and that fortification is the stronger of the two factors. Both the principal component analysis and the cluster analysis identified fortification, and not variety, as the main source of variation in product quality, while variety operated at a second level within each product group.

The three aromatic landraces were superior to the non-aromatic check Dudeshwar for protein, phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant potential and every sensory attribute examined. This provides a sound nutritional justification, in addition to the cultural and aromatic value already recognised, for the continued cultivation and conservation of these landraces. Among them Kalojira was the richest in the bioactive fractions, Gobindabhog carried the best mineral profile with the lowest phytate load, and Radhunipagal gave the softest product with the highest iron and zinc.

Fortification with beet extract raised total phenol about three fold, antioxidant activity about two fold and calcium about six fold, and was the sole source of anthocyanin, while fortification with carrot extract was the sole source of beta-carotene and gave the highest resistant starch with the lowest predicted glycaemic index. Both treatments softened the product, improved its colour and raised its acceptability, and did so to the same extent in every variety. The gain in minerals is, however, partly offset by an accompanying rise in phytate, so the phytate to mineral ratio rather than the mineral content alone should be used to judge the nutritional value of the fortified product.

On the basis of overall performance, KBI, that is idli prepared from Kalojira and fortified with beet extract, is recommended as the best combination, since it recorded the highest total phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant activity, soluble protein, anthocyanin and overall acceptability. KCI is recommended where a provitamin A rich product of low glycaemic response is required and GBI where a mineral enriched product is required. The plain product of the non-aromatic check was the poorest treatment for almost every character examined and is not suited to this purpose.

The wider significance of these findings is that a traditional fermented food can be enriched in phenolics, antioxidants, provitamin A and minerals using nothing more than two commonly available vegetables, without recourse to any synthetic colourant, additive or fortificant, and without any loss of consumer acceptance. This offers a practical route for adding value to the aromatic rice landraces of West Bengal and for improving the nutritional quality of a food that is consumed daily by a large population.

Certain limitations should be recognised. The study was confined to four varieties and to a single level of fortification, and the sensory evaluation was carried out by a semi-trained panel rather than a consumer panel. The bioaccessibility of the added minerals and pigments was not measured directly, and the shelf life and microbiological stability of the fortified batter were not examined. Further work may therefore be directed towards optimising the level of vegetable extract, measuring the in vitro bioaccessibility of the added iron, zinc and calcium in the presence of the observed phytate, characterising the individual phenolic acids and betalains by chromatographic methods, and evaluating the storage behaviour and consumer acceptance of the fortified product on a larger scale.
